summary: FT profile (Nov 2016) of David Harding: how Winton invests. Method: interview; no data. Message: exploit many weak, renewable statistical signals across broad markets, grounded in behavioural failures of efficient markets.

coverage.note: nothing actionable: full-page portrait photo (checked image)
weak signals, breadth, weather/inventory/seasonal signals, decay, EMH critique, research process; philanthropy and tax paragraphs not actionable

claims.speaker: Clive Cookson (FT journalist)
claims.quote: Harding’s idea was that finance could use science to identify and exploit inefficiencies in the markets.
claims.claim: Scientific and mathematical methods can find and exploit market inefficiencies (Harding 1994 Royal Society paper "Making money from mathematical models").

claims.speaker: Clive Cookson (FT journalist)
claims.quote: manages $32bn of assets
claims.claim: Winton managed about $32bn in 2016, showing the approach scales to large capacity.

claims.speaker: David Harding (interviewed)
claims.quote: The aim is to exploit a large number of weak predictive signals
claims.claim: Winton combines many weak predictive signals across a broad universe rather than relying on a few strong ones.
claims.exact_rule: Combine many weak signals across many instruments (breadth over signal strength); specifics not given

claims.speaker: David Harding (interviewed)
claims.quote: if there are strong relationships, someone else is going to be exploiting those. Weak relationships are where we have a competitive advantage.
claims.claim: Strong predictive relationships get arbitraged away by competitors, so the remaining edge lies in many weak relationships.

claims.speaker: Clive Cookson (FT journalist)
claims.quote: covering bonds, currencies, commodities, market indices and individual equi- ties.
claims.claim: The universe spans bonds, currencies, commodities, equity indices and single stocks, giving breadth for weak signals.
claims.exact_rule: Universe: bonds, FX, commodities, equity index futures, single equities

claims.speaker: Clive Cookson (FT journalist)
claims.quote: analysis of cloud cover and soil moisture levels to predict the prices of agricultural commodities.
claims.claim: Weather data such as cloud cover and soil moisture are used to forecast agricultural commodity prices.
claims.data_needed: satellite/weather data: cloud cover, soil moisture; agricultural futures prices
claims.direction: supply shock forecasts -> ag price direction (unspecified)
claims.testable: yes - weather data vs crop futures

claims.speaker: Clive Cookson (FT journalist)
claims.quote: Other important indicators, for which maths can uncover value not fully reflected in market prices, include seasonal factors and inventory levels across supply chains.
claims.claim: Seasonal patterns and supply-chain inventory levels carry price information not fully priced in markets.
claims.data_needed: inventory data across supply chains; seasonal price history
claims.testable: yes - inventory and seasonality signals testable

claims.speaker: Clive Cookson (FT journalist)
claims.quote: Harding admits to using science and mathemat- ics as a marketing tool
claims.claim: Harding concedes the science framing is partly marketing, while insisting science controls the strategy.

claims.speaker: David Harding (interviewed)
claims.quote: eventually what we discovered would leak out
claims.claim: Research discoveries leak to competitors over time, so edges decay even when kept secret.

claims.speaker: Clive Cookson (FT journalist)
claims.quote: Those clients have seen a compound annual growth rate of 12.8 per cent, net of fees.
claims.claim: Winton clients earned 12.8% a year compounded, net of fees (period not stated, presumably since 1997).
claims.reported_result: CAGR 12.8% net of fees (period unstated, fund unstated)

claims.speaker: unnamed quantitative fund manager (quoted)
claims.quote: I would estimate that systematic or mathe- matical funds amount to 15 per cent of assets in the hedge fund industry
claims.claim: Another quant manager estimates systematic funds at about 15% of hedge fund assets, $330-450bn.

claims.speaker: David Harding (interviewed)
claims.quote: we have used techniques that would be described as machine learning for at least 30 years.
claims.claim: Winton has used what is now called machine learning for decades; the AI excitement is not new to quant investing.

claims.speaker: Clive Cookson (FT journalist)
claims.quote: This is a never- ending process because predictive tools lose their power as markets change; new ones are always needed.
claims.claim: Predictive signals lose power as markets change, so research must continually find new signals.

claims.speaker: David Harding (interviewed)
claims.quote: We have 450 people in the company, of whom 250 are involved in research, data collection or technology
claims.claim: Most staff (250 of 450) work in research, data or technology, reflecting the resource cost of continual signal renewal.

claims.speaker: Clive Cookson (FT journalist)
claims.quote: in 1987, he co-founded AHL as a commodities trading firm with two other young physicists
claims.claim: Harding co-founded AHL (1987, sold to Man Group 1994) and founded Winton in 1997 on empirical research.

claims.speaker: Clive Cookson (FT journalist)
claims.quote: these methods consist essentially of selling complex derivatives at marked-up prices and of arbitrage
claims.claim: Banks and brokers mainly earn from fees, marked-up derivatives and arbitrage, unlike prediction-based investing.

claims.speaker: David Harding (interviewed)
claims.quote: It treats economics like a physical science when, in fact, it is a human or social science.
claims.claim: Efficient market theory is wrong because economics is a human science, not a physical one.

claims.speaker: David Harding (interviewed)
claims.quote: Humans are prone to unpredictable behaviour, to over-reaction or slumbering inaction, to mania and panic.
claims.claim: Human over-reaction, under-reaction (slumbering inaction), mania and panic create exploitable price patterns.

claims.speaker: David Harding (interviewed)
claims.quote: We don’t make assumptions about how markets should work, rather we use advanced statistical techniques to seek patterns in huge datasets
claims.claim: Winton is empirical: it does not assume how markets work but searches large datasets statistically for patterns.

claims.speaker: David Harding (interviewed)
claims.quote: making observa- tions and developing hypotheses and then testing these hypotheses against empirical evidence.
claims.claim: Research follows the scientific method: organise data, observe, hypothesise, then test against evidence.

reasoning.question: How does a large systematic fund (Winton) make money from markets, and what is its research philosophy?

thesis.statement: Markets are imperfect because humans over-react, under-react and panic; strong inefficiencies get arbitraged away, so a scientific, empirical process that combines many weak signals across many markets and keeps renewing them is the source of edge.

foundations.premise: Markets are not efficient because economics is a human science with over-reaction, inaction, mania and panic.
Strong predictive relationships are competed away.

mechanism_chain.to: patterns in prices not fully reflecting information

mechanism_chain.from: many weak signals across broad universe
mechanism_chain.why: (reader) breadth: many small independent edges add up

design_rationale.choice: Many weak signals instead of few strong ones
Alternative data: weather, inventories, seasonality for commodities
design_rationale.reason_given: value not fully reflected in prices

design_rationale.choice: Assumption-free statistical pattern search / scientific method
design_rationale.reason_given: EMH is wrong; let data speak

evidence_map.does_not_rule_out: (reader) returns may be mostly trend following beta; period, vol and drawdowns unstated; survivorship of a famous manager

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: No signal definitions, horizons or weights; journalistic profile
Assumption-free pattern search conflicts with need to avoid data mining; no out-of-sample discipline described
Science framing partly marketing by own admission

relations.why: (reader) "slumbering inaction" is the behavioural basis of trend; Winton/AHL were trend followers

reasoning.forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Weather (soil moisture, cloud cover) and supply-chain inventories lead agricultural and other commodity prices over weeks to months via supply surprises; seasonal factors lead via recurring patterns. These stop working when widely exploited (crowding) or when market structure changes.
reader_inferences: (reader) The weak-signals-plus-breadth logic is the fundamental law of active management (IR ~ IC x sqrt(breadth)), not named in the article.
(reader) Over-reaction and slumbering inaction map to reversal and momentum respectively.
(reader) The article is a profile, so its evidential value is low; use only as design philosophy.
